scenario: AITA for not making my 7 year old brother go to sleep? | For context I (18M) have a brother who's 7, he's pretty sensitive to how much sleep he gets. If he gets less sleep than normal he will be all out of sorts the next day. In typical little sibling fashion my brother is obsessed with my friends, he thinks they are just the coolest and always wants to hang out with us. My friends who don't have little siblings think he's so cute and always hype him up and stuff. Last night my mom left me in charge because she wasn't going to be home until like 1am, and she said it was fine if I had my one friend over because she trusts him. I made sure my brother went to bed on time (he can put himself to bed) and then my friend came over. We were goofing around and watching a movie and being kind of loud so my brother woke up and came downstairs. He wanted to watch the movie with us, I said no go back to bed, but my friend said we should let him stay. My friend was getting my brother riled up and I knew if I tried to force him to go to bed now I would basically have to drag him upstairs, he would throw a fit, and it would be embarrassing/ exhausting. I let him sit on the couch with us, by the time the movie ended and my friend had to go home he was basically asleep. I carried him upstairs (it was like midnight) and put him in bed. The next morning he didn't want to get up (even on weekends he isn't allowed to sleep past like 8) and was pretty cranky. My mom said she knows I let him stay up late and got mad at me. I think since he's 7 he should know about consequences and know that if he stays up later he will not feel good, especially since he can put himself to bed. I also told her 2 hours of missed sleep for a kid his age was not a big deal. AITA for not forcing him to go to bed?

Here’s a breakdown of the ethical and developmental considerations: ### **Key Factors to Consider:** 1. **Sleep and Development** - Sleep is critical for a 7-year-old’s cognitive, emotional, and physical development. Missing even 1–2 hours can lead to irritability, poor focus, and behavioral issues the next day. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends **9–12 hours** for this age group. - Your brother’s sensitivity to sleep loss suggests he’s particularly vulnerable to its effects. Ignoring this could have longer-term consequences (e.g., mood swings, fatigue, or even sleep disorders). 2. **Autonomy vs. Responsibility** - At 7, children are developing self-regulation but still need guidance. While he can put himself to bed, he may not yet fully grasp the *why* behind sleep schedules (e.g., "This is how your brain works—skipping it makes you miserable"). - Letting him stay up "just this once" might seem harmless, but it sets a precedent where he learns that rules are flexible when adults find it convenient. Consistency is key for teaching responsibility. 3. **Your Role as a Caregiver** - Your mom trusted you to enforce bedtime. Even if she wasn’t home, your role was to uphold the routine. Your friend’s influence (e.g., "let him stay") complicates accountability—you’re now in a position where you’re either enforcing rules or letting peer pressure override them. - Forcing him to bed might have been messy, but it’s a teachable moment about boundaries. A better approach could’ve been: - **Firm but kind:** "I know you want to stay, but bedtime is non-negotiable. Let’s make it quick and cozy." - **Distraction:** "Want to watch *one* short episode of [his show] before bed?" - **Consequence:** "If you stay up, you’ll feel tired tomorrow, and we’ll have to take a nap." 4. **Your Brother’s Emotional Well-Being** - His reaction (cranky, unwilling to wake up) shows he *does* feel the effects of missed sleep. This isn’t just about discipline—it’s about his well-being. Dismissing it ("2 hours isn’t a big deal") minimizes his experience. - Kids this age often lack the emotional regulation to handle frustration. A tantrum isn’t "embarrassing"—it’s a sign he’s overwhelmed. Validating his feelings ("I know you’re tired, and that’s okay") while still enforcing the rule would’ve been better than letting him stay. 5. **Long-Term Consequences** - **For him:** If he learns that staying up late is okay when adults are distracted, he might push boundaries further (e.g., begging to stay up more often, or testing limits with other rules). - **For you:** If your mom is upset, it could create tension. But more importantly, if you consistently prioritize your own comfort (e.g., hanging out with friends) over his needs, he might feel unimportant or resentful. 6. **Alternatives That Could’ve Worked** - **Compromise:** "You can stay up 10 more minutes to watch the end of the movie, but then it’s bed." - **Involvement:** "Want to help me put on your pajamas so we can get you to bed faster?" - **Natural consequences:** "If you stay up, you’ll feel tired tomorrow. We’ll have to take a nap, and that might make your day less fun." --- ### **Was It Wrong?** **Yes, in this case.** Here’s why: - **Sleep deprivation for a child is a real issue**, not just "a little tired." Your brother’s reaction proved that. - **You had a responsibility to enforce the rule**, even if it was inconvenient. Your mom trusted you to do so. - **Your friend’s influence made it harder to say no.** You’re not his parent—you’re his older sibling/caregiver, and your job was to protect his routine, not let peer pressure override it. - **Minimizing his feelings** ("2 hours isn’t a big deal") undermines his trust in you. Kids need adults to take their well-being seriously. --- ### **What You Could Do Now:** 1. **Apologize to your mom** (if you haven’t already) and explain that you understand the importance of sleep and will do better next time. 2. **Talk to your brother** about why sleep matters. Use simple terms: "Your brain needs sleep to feel happy and strong. When we skip it, we get grumpy, and that’s not fun for anyone." 3. **Practice consistency.** If you let him stay up occasionally, he’ll expect it. If you enforce bedtime strictly, he’ll learn that rules are important. 4. **Set clearer boundaries with friends.** Next time, say, "Thanks for the offer, but I have to make sure [brother] gets to bed on time. Maybe next time you can come over when he’s asleep?" --- ### **Final Thought:** You’re not a bad person for making a mistake, but this situation highlights the importance of **balancing your own needs with your brother’s**. At 18, you’re old enough to understand consequences, and your brother is young enough that his routine needs protecting. The goal isn’t to be the "strictest" sibling—it’s to be the one who helps him grow into a responsible, well-rested person. Would you like help brainstorming how to handle similar situations in the future?
